title: Wrexham 2 Chelsea 4 – VAR woe for hosts, superb Doyle flick, lucky escape for Blues?
author: Simon Johnson
content:
Chelsea are into the FA Cup quarter-finals, but only after enduring a mighty scare from 10-man Championship side Wrexham in a six-goal thriller that went to extra-time at The Racecourse Ground.

Wrexham took the lead through Sam Smith after 18 minutes and frustrated a much-changed Chelsea until Alejandro Garnacho’s goal-bound shot found its way into the home net with the help of a hugely unfortunate ricochet off the back of goalkeeper Arthur Okonkwo.

Callum Doyle restored Wrexham’s advantage in the 78th minute, only for Josh Acheampong to smash Chelsea level four minutes later. With extra time beckoning, George Dobson was shown a straight red card by referee Peter Bankes for a late lunge on Garnacho after a VAR review.

Garnacho then swept Chelsea in front six minutes into extra time from Dario Essugo’s cross, but the Premier League side were never comfortable despite the extra man and Lewis Brunt briefly thought he had nodded Wrexham level from a corner kick, but VAR confirmed he was marginally offside.

Joao Pedro then fired a low shot into the bottom corner with just about the last kick of the match to give Chelsea a 4-2 margin of victory that their performance scarcely deserved against impressive second-tier opposition.

For a few seconds, it seemed as if Dobson would get away with the kind of tackle that many defenders have considered subjecting Garnacho to in recent years.

Ref Bankes initially ignored the wide-eyed protests of several Chelsea players to flash only his yellow card as Garnacho writhed, grimacing on the floor and clutching his left leg. But then Dobson and Wrexham, who play in the VAR-free Football League, got their introduction to football in the age of the all-seeing eye.

Video assistant referee Paul Howard got in touch to recommend that Bankes review Dobson’s challenge on the pitchside monitor, as serious foul play (a straight red card offence) may have been missed. That he had caught the Argentina international high and late midway up the shin was not in dispute; the brief conversation between the two officials focused on the speed of the tackle.

His eyes trained on numerous replays and with Howard in his ear, Bankes did not take much convincing.

“After review, Wrexham No 15 catches his opponent high with intensity,” he told the crowd on his return to the pitch. “The final decision is a red card for serious foul play.”

On a normal Championship matchday at The Racecourse, Dobson would have escaped such an incident with a booking. But if Wrexham make it to the Premier League sooner rather than later, they will need to get used to the fact that such fouls do not elude VAR.

Neither do offsides, no matter how marginal.

The tip of Brunt’s left foot was all that ventured beyond Chelsea’s defensive line as Kieffer Moore flicked an in-swinging corner kick across the face of goal, and the home supporters were entitled to roar with delight as Brunt nodded the ball in at the back post to seemingly make it 3-3 deep in extra time.

Moore’s initial contact was not going in, and once the digital lines were drawn, there could be no complaints — even if denying 10-man Wrexham a dramatic equaliser, potentially taking this tie to a penalty shootout, felt wrong on a karmic level.

‘F**k VAR’, the Wrexham fans sang over and over.

It’s safe to say they did not enjoy their first taste of video intervention.

Liam Twomey

The scenes outside the Wrexham Lager Stand beforehand, as the home team’s players mingled with fans, signing autographs and posing for photographs, felt like a throwback to a more wholesome era, as did an FA Cup tie that carried all the drama, tension and atmosphere of the competition’s heyday.

What we got was an FA Cup classic — not just in terms of the way the game transpired, with so many twists and turns, but in terms of the occasion.

For all the inevitable focus on the “Hollywood” angle, with the TV cameras repeatedly drawn to Wrexham’s co-owners Ryan Reynolds and Rob Mac watching in the VIP area, the atmosphere all-round was raw and passionate. From the very start, Chelsea’s players knew they were not going to be playing in any kind of comfort zone.

Roared on by the crowd, Wrexham’s players fought for every ball, desperate to add another Premier League scalp after their third-round victory here against Nottingham Forest. In the end, Chelsea’s superior fitness and quality from the bench told — as did, significantly, the extra man once Dobson was sent off for that wild challenge on Garnacho — but the occasion will have given the home supporters and players another taste of the big time and left them longing for more.

Liam Rosenior is a fortunate man this evening — he gambled with his team selection and it paid off… just.

The timing of this fixture was always going to pose a challenge for the Chelsea head coach in terms of how many changes to make, and surely he will have to concede post-game that nine was too many.

With this FA Cup tie sandwiched between a must-win Premier League game at Aston Villa three days ago and the first leg of a Champions League last-16 meeting with holders Paris Saint-Germain in the French capital on Wednesday, Rosenior did need to rotate his squad.

However, after selecting seven defensive-minded outfield players among the 10 starters, it was no wonder Chelsea laboured in attack for large parts of this game. With only Liam Delap, Pedro Neto and Garnacho to mark for just under an hour, Wrexham’s red wall was rarely penetrated.

Chelsea were fortunate to go in at half-time with the scores level at 1-1, needing a bit of luck when a clearance hit goalkeeper Okonkwo and ended up in the Wrexham net.

And even when Rosenior did start to change it, third-choice striker Marc Guiu was the change, rather than in-form Joao Pedro, who eventually entered the fray at 2-2 with just five minutes of normal time remaining. The Brazilian’s impact was instant, making those of a Chelsea persuasion wonder why a player who has scored 10 goals in his previous 11 appearances was left watching on for so long.

Experienced duo Marc Cucurella and Malo Gusto also came on after the interval, but the sight of midfielder Dario Essugo making what was his first appearance of the season due to injury also betrayed how Rosenior’s priority was PSG rather than Wrexham.

With the tie going to extra time, the plan to give the likes of Joao Pedro, Gusto and Cucurella a comfortable and restful evening backfired anyway. Neto and Garnacho, Chelsea’s only fit wingers at the moment, will surely feel the strain of playing 100 and 120 minutes respectively here.

Chelsea have not won a domestic trophy since the 2017-18 FA Cup and getting drawn against Championship opposition, albeit a club on the rise, in round five was a golden opportunity to reach next month’s quarter-finals. Their hopes are still alive, but that is perhaps more down to luck than judgement.

Simon Johnson

Hollywood loves a sequel, and the hope for everyone at Wrexham is that this fixture is one we’ll be seeing again in the not-too-distant future — in the Premier League.

This really was a night to savour for the Welsh club co-owned by Ryan Reynolds and Rob Mac, even allowing for how it ultimately ended in VAR-induced disappointment.

Wrexham were superb, tearing into Chelsea from the very start to maintain The Racecourse Ground’s reputation as the place to be for thrills and spills, and plenty of goals.

Even before this latest shootout, Wrexham had the unusual distinction of having scored more goals on home soil in the 2025-26 Championship (33) than everyone except leaders Coventry City and fourth-placed Ipswich Town but also conceded more in their backyard (28) than any of their second-tier peers bar Hull City and already-relegated Sheffield Wednesday.

Throw in 3-3 draws against visitors Hull and Forest in knockout football, and it was perhaps no surprise just how entertaining the first meeting with Chelsea here since February 1982 proved.

Manager Phil Parkinson’s side deserve huge credit for this, particularly in a game where their illustrious visitors enjoyed 68 per cent of the possession.

Allowing Chelsea to pass the ball among themselves along the back line was clearly the plan, providing that, once play moved up into midfield, the hosts were ready to pounce.

As two fizzing balls of energy, Ollie Rathbone and Lewis O’Brien, deployed as the pair of No 10s playing off lone striker Smith in a 3-4-2-1 set-up, were perfect for this plan. Their constant hassling and harrying, plus the problems Smith caused for Tosin Adarabioyo, provided the platform for a night when the world club champions were given an almighty scare.

Once that trio had run themselves into the ground, substitutes Moore, Josh Windass and Nathan Broadhead took over to keep the pressure on.

Wrexham’s goals were pretty special, too. First, Doyle’s floated pass allowed Smith to leave Tosin trailing before finishing coolly past Robert Sanchez. Then, the provider turned scorer, as Doyle’s quite exquisite flick of the heel diverted Windass’ shot past the helpless ’keeper.

But for Dobson’s red card in second-half stoppage time, who knows how things may have panned out?

Maybe Chelsea would have had the quality to go through anyway. Or, maybe Wrexham would have gone on to claim another notable cup scalp. We’ll never know.

But surely a repeat of this fixture in the Premier League would be box-office stuff. Over to Parkinson and his side, currently in the Championship’s play-off places, to make that happen.

Richard Sutcliffe

Rosenior was quick to publicly praise Sanchez’s “magnificent” reaction in training to being benched for understudy Filip Jorgensen in Chelsea’s 4-1 win at Villa on Wednesday, but the response that matters most for any footballer is the one they deliver on the pitch.

On one level, starting against Wrexham rubber-stamped Sanchez’s demotion to cup-goalkeeper status. It also provided an immediate opportunity to demonstrate that he has steadied his form in time for Rosenior to regard him as a reliable option for the final stretch of Chelsea’s season.

The Spaniard did not take it.

Rosenior opting to match systems with Wrexham — a decision informed as much by available personnel as by tactical need — gave Sanchez plenty of protection in the early going. Chelsea’s passing was safe and sideways, and their Championship hosts snapped forward whenever they could, but it was not at all clear how they could hope to score.

Then the 18th minute happened.

Doyle’s floated ball over the Chelsea defence first exposed Tosin’s crippling lack of speed, then Sanchez’s unfortunate penchant for indecision in key moments. He advanced from his goal, causing the recovering Benoit Badiashile to hesitate, then retreated, leaving himself caught in no-man’s land.

Some may point to his raking pass to the feet of Delap in the lead-up to Chelsea’s equaliser as Sanchez’s redemptive contribution, but a closer look revealed that it was fortunate not to be intercepted by Wrexham.

There was nothing Sanchez could do about Doyle’s brilliantly improvised goal, not that it matters much in the final reckoning.

No position on the pitch is as brutally appraised as goalkeeper, and the key moments in games are everything. The burden was on Sanchez here to make Rosenior rethink his selection choice against Villa, and he did not meet it.

Liam Twomey

We will bring you this after he has spoken at the post-match press conference.
